config.title: Build finite state machine for UI states

intro.title: Build finite state machine for UI states
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple finite state machine (FSM) to manage the different states of a user interface, like 'idle', 'loading', 'success', and 'error'. You'll learn how to use a JavaScript object to define the possible states and transitions, and a function to change the current state based on rules. The main technologies involved are JavaScript objects, functions, and conditional logic. By the end, you'll have a working FSM that controls UI behavior, helping you understand how to organize and predict state changes in your applications.
intro.usecase: Finite state machines are essential for managing predictable UI behavior in real-world applications. For example, a multi-step checkout form transitions between states like 'entering details', 'validating payment', and 'order confirmation'. Similarly, a dashboard's data filter panel might cycle through 'collapsed', 'loading options', and 'expanded with results'. This pattern prevents invalid state combinations, making complex UI logic easier to debug and maintain.

objectives: Implement a finite state machine to manage UI state transitions
Apply state transition logic to control UI behavior
Construct a state object that defines all possible UI states
Configure event handlers to trigger state changes
Manipulate DOM elements based on the current state
Initialize the state machine with a default UI state
Render UI components conditionally according to state values

import React, { useState } from 'react';

successCriteria: The component is named StateMachineUI and returns a JSX div element.

steps.title: Define the finite state machine states
steps.instruction: Inside your StateMachineUI component, create a constant object named 'states' that defines the possible UI states: IDLE, LOADING, SUCCESS, and ERROR.
steps.hint: Define an object with string values for each state. For example: const states = { IDLE: 'idle', LOADING: 'loading' }
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a 'states' object with four properties: IDLE, LOADING, SUCCESS, and ERROR, each with string values representing the state names.
successCriteria: A 'states' constant object is defined inside the component with IDLE, LOADING, SUCCESS, and ERROR properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've defined all four states: IDLE, LOADING, SUCCESS, and ERROR as properties of a 'states' object.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try creating a constant object named 'states' with properties for IDLE, LOADING, SUCCESS, and ERROR. Each property should have a string value representing that state.

steps.title: Initialize the current state
steps.instruction: Inside your StateMachineUI component, initialize a state variable called currentState using useState. Set its initial value to 'IDLE'.
steps.hint: Call useState with 'IDLE' as the initial argument, and destructure the returned array into currentState and a setter function.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: initializing state
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a state variable currentState initialized to 'IDLE', ready to track the UI's current state.
successCriteria: The useState hook is called with 'IDLE' as the initial value, and the returned array is destructured into currentState and a setter function.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're calling useState with 'IDLE' as the initial value and destructuring the returned array into currentState and a setter.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't match what we need. Initialize a state variable called currentState with useState, starting with the value 'IDLE'.

steps.title: Add state transition buttons
steps.instruction: Inside your component, add three buttons before the closing tag. Each button should have an onClick handler that calls setCurrentState with the appropriate state string: 'LOADING', 'SUCCESS', and 'ERROR'. Label them 'Start Loading', 'Mark Success', and 'Mark Error' respectively.
steps.hint: Create <button> elements with onClick={() => setCurrentState('STATE_NAME')} and appropriate text content.
steps.expectedOutcome: Three buttons appear in the UI that, when clicked, will change the currentState to LOADING, SUCCESS, or ERROR.
successCriteria: Three <button> elements are added with onClick handlers calling setCurrentState with the correct state strings and appropriate labels.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added some buttons, but check that all three are present with the correct onClick handlers and labels: LOADING, SUCCESS, ERROR.
steps.feedbackWrong: The buttons aren't set up correctly. Make sure you have three <button> elements with onClick handlers that call setCurrentState with the state strings 'LOADING', 'SUCCESS', and 'ERROR'.

steps.title: Wire buttons to transition functions
steps.instruction: Add onClick handlers to each button that call the appropriate transition function.
steps.hint: Use the onClick attribute on each button to call the corresponding transition function you created earlier.

<button onClick={handleClick}>Click me</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: Each button will have an onClick handler that triggers the corresponding state transition when clicked.
successCriteria: All four buttons have onClick handlers that call the appropriate transition functions (transitionToLoading, transitionToSuccess, transitionToError, resetState).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.

successCriteria: The Reset button has an onClick handler that calls resetState.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added an onClick handler, but make sure it calls the resetState function correctly.

steps.title: Add conditional UI based on state
steps.instruction: Inside your component's return statement, add conditional rendering that displays different messages for each state. Use the currentState variable to show different UI content for 'IDLE', 'LOADING', 'SUCCESS', and 'ERROR' states.
steps.hint: You can use if/else statements, switch statements, or ternary operators inside JSX to conditionally render different content based on currentState.
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will now show different messages or content depending on which state the finite state machine is in, making the state changes visually apparent to the user.
successCriteria: Conditional rendering is implemented that displays different UI content for each possible state ('IDLE', 'LOADING', 'SUCCESS', 'ERROR').
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some conditional logic, but make sure you handle all four states ('IDLE', 'LOADING', 'SUCCESS', 'ERROR') with appropriate UI content for each.
steps.feedbackWrong: The conditional rendering isn't working correctly. Make sure you're checking the currentState variable and rendering different content for each possible state value.
